analysis.one_liner: Removed the legal shield that protects government officials from being personally sued for violating constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 41 House cosponsors and would have removed qualified immunity from federal civil-rights lawsuits, never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone's constitutional rights are violated by a police officer or other government official, they can sue the official for damages. But courts have created a doctrine called "qualified immunity" that lets officials escape liability unless a prior court decision clearly established that the exact conduct was illegal — which makes many lawsuits fail. This bill would have removed that defense, restoring the standard that existed from the civil-rights law's founding in 1871 until the Supreme Court created the doctrine in 1967. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, but no hearing or vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by police officers, prison guards, and other state or local government officials would be able to sue for damages even when no court has previously ruled the exact conduct illegal. This includes victims of excessive force and other misconduct who currently lose their cases on qualified-immunity grounds before a jury ever hears the facts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police and government misconduct

how_it_helps.text: The bill added language to the federal civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) stating that neither good faith, nor a belief that the conduct was lawful, nor the absence of a clearly established right could be used as a defense in a civil-rights lawsuit.

By eliminating qualified immunity, the bill would have allowed people whose constitutional rights were violated by state and local officials to recover damages even when no prior court decision had specifically outlawed the exact conduct in question.

The bill's findings section documented that the doctrine was created by the Supreme Court starting in 1967, not by Congress, and argued that it had 'severely limited the ability of many plaintiffs to recover damages' under the statute.

analysis.who_pays: Police officers, government officials, and their employers would face personal liability in lawsuits for constitutional violations, with no good-faith defense, and would bear higher litigation and insurance costs. Taxpayers could also bear costs where governments indemnify their employees.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued that removing qualified immunity would expose police officers, teachers, and other government workers to personal lawsuits even when they acted in good faith, which they said could make people hesitant to do their jobs.
The bill applied retroactively to any suit pending on its effective date, not just new cases, which meant past conduct could draw new liability.

The bill did not address any of the other barriers plaintiffs face in civil-rights cases, such as the difficulty of winning damages even where liability is established, and offered no mechanism for governments to indemnify employees instead of leaving them personally exposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have restored a meaningful legal remedy for constitutional violations by government officials, at the cost of exposing those officials to personal liability even in close cases. Honest supporters would acknowledge the strongest objection: without the clearly-established standard, officials might hesitate to act in uncertain situations, and the bill applied retroactively to suits already pending. An honest accounting also notes the bill went no further than restoring the standard that applied from 1871 through the 1960s. On the other side, the bill was one-sided: it offered no funding for training, no mechanism to indemnify officers through employers, and no alternative path to accountability. The central fact, though, is that none of these trade-offs were ever debated on the floor; the bill died without a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, but the committee never voted on it and it never reached the House floor, dying when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 1, 2021 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee.
On April 28, 2021 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials who violate constitutional rights keep their qualified-immunity shield from personal lawsuits. Because the bill never received a hearing or a vote, no member ever had to go on record on the substance.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act on March 1, 2021.

for.name: 41 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican support.

against.name: Police unions and law-enforcement organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed ending qualified immunity during the 2021 policing debates.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee in April 2021 and never advanced it to a markup or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported it, though the decisive step was a Democratic-led committee never scheduling it.

industries.note: Qualified immunity shields individual officers from paying damages in civil-rights lawsuits; the bill would have removed that shield and made officers personally answerable for constitutional violations. Police organizations opposed its Senate companion in the 117th Congress. Sources: [S2], [S3].

Governments would likely face more civil-rights litigation and would face pressure to indemnify or insure their employees against the new personal liability. Some cities would also benefit from clearer legal standards and fewer dismissed claims. Sources: [S2], [S3].
